questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the office because of a 1-month history of intermittent sharp pain of the ring and small fingers of his right hand. He does not recall any trauma to the hand and has not had fever, weakness, chills, or rash. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He is right-hand dominant. He plays varsity basketball and pitches for the varsity baseball team. He has a part-time after-school job bagging groceries at a local store. His mother has moderately severe rheumatoid arthritis. The patient’s vital signs are within normal limits. Both wrists and hands appear normal. Muscle strength is 5/5 in the upper extremities. Range of motion of the shoulders, elbows, wrists, and finger joints is full bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s pain?

questions.subject: Neurology
questions.explanation: Ulnar tunnel syndrome, or cubital tunnel syndrome, is a neuropathy of the ulnar nerve occurring at the level of the elbow. The ulnar nerve innervates the intrinsic muscles of the hand (eg, lumbricals, interossei, hypothenar, and palmaris brevis) and muscles of the forearm (eg, flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar portion of flexor digitorum profundus). The ulnar nerve also provides sensation to the volar aspects of the ring and small finger. Patients with ulnar tunnel syndrome most commonly present with sensory symptoms, with more severe cases presenting with hand intrinsic muscle weakness or claw hand deformity. In this case, the patient most likely developed ulnar neuropathy at the elbow from repetitive pitching. Other risk factors include prolonged leaning on elbows, repetitive forearm pronation/supination, or activities that require repetitive grip. Diagnosis can be confirmed with electromyography and nerve conduction studies. Treatment is usually conservative, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

wrongAnswers.A: Occupational tasks (Choice A) that include repetitive grip or pronation/supination activities can be a risk factor for developing ulnar tunnel syndrome. This patient is age 16 years with a part-time job bagging groceries. Because of the part-time nature of his job, his position as a pitcher on the baseball team is a more likely cause of his pain.
wrongAnswers.B: Osteoarthritis (Choice B) is a degenerative condition affecting the articular cartilage of joints and is one of the most common diseases afflicting adults. Repetitive use, such as in heavy labor, is a common risk factor. In the case of an otherwise healthy 16-year-old boy, sports activities are a more likely cause of his current symptoms.
wrongAnswers.D: Synovial crystal deposition (Choice D) occurs in cases of gout and pseudogout. Gout is an inflammatory arthropathy incited by hyperuricemia with deposition of uric acid crystals inside the joint and surrounding tissues. This type of arthritis typically presents following consumption of a purine-rich meal or alcohol (which competes with kidney excretion of uric acid). This patient is an otherwise healthy 16-year-old boy without localized findings on physical examination, making ulnar tunnel syndrome brought on by sports activities more likely.
wrongAnswers.E: The cause is idiopathic (Choice E) could be a reasonable choice in cases of juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis occurs before age 16 years and is a common rheumatic disease among children. The disease has an autoimmune cause and is characterized by joint pain and inflammation. Patients commonly exhibit extra-articular manifestations such as uveitis, lymphadenopathy, and rash. In this case, the patient has localized findings of sensory deficits over the ring and small fingers, with other findings within normal limits on examination. The cause of this patient’s symptoms is most likely ulnar tunnel syndrome brought on by sports activities.

questions.stem: Six hours after a 10-year-old boy undergoes operative repair of a humerus fracture, his parents notice that he is unresponsive and barely breathing and notify the nursing staff. The patient has no history of serious illness. His only medication is intravenous morphine. On evaluation, he is unconscious. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 90/50 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 88%. The pupils are 2 mm. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Intravenous naloxone is administered, and the patient regains consciousness. His respirations now are 18/min. It is most appropriate for the hospital to investigate this incident as which of the following?

questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences
questions.explanation: This patient received too much opioid medication, resulting in decreased consciousness and life-threatening respiratory suppression. This incident can be defined as a sentinel event, a patient safety event resulting in death, permanent harm, or temporary serious harm that may require life-sustaining treatment (eg, naloxone). Sentinel events typically prompt a root cause analysis (RCA) to determine the factors contributing to the adverse event. RCA involves determining the core systems-level issues that lead to the chain reaction of events that culminate in the adverse event. There are several RCA strategies, including creating a timeline, surveying the controls in place that may have failed, and completing a risk tree analysis where the impact of each event is considered. A multidisciplinary team commonly works to define and analyze the problem and design a set of corrective actions based on the analysis.

wrongAnswers.B: Improper hand-off (Choice B) refers to inadequate communication between healthcare professionals about a patient care situation. Improper handoffs are a common cause of adverse patient safety events. Though RCA may ultimately detail communication difficulties causing the sentinel event in this case, inadequate communication is not mentioned in the case description.
wrongAnswers.C: Perioperative risk (Choice C) refers to the risk for perioperative adverse patient safety events. Risk implies a hypothetical event. The case describes the occurrence of a real event, not a hypothetical event. Adverse events related to opioids are relatively rare if titrated appropriately.
wrongAnswers.D: Quality indicator (Choice D) refers to a measure of healthcare quality. Examples include staffing ratios and the number of board-certified physicians in a hospital. Sentinel events are commonly related to poor scores on quality indicators but are not defined as quality indicators.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of progressive urinary frequency and decreased urinary stream. He underwent transurethral resection of the prostate 11 years ago because of benign hyperplasia. He takes no medications. Examination shows a moderately enlarged prostate. His serum creatinine concentration has increased from 1.3 mg/dL 10 months ago to 2.4 mg/dL today. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology
questions.explanation: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) affects middle-aged and elderly male patients and occurs as a result of excess growth of tissue in the central zone of the prostate causing lower urinary tract obstruction. BPH presents with urinary dribbling and incontinence, difficulty starting or maintaining a urinary stream, nocturia, the need to frequently urinate, and incomplete voiding. These symptoms are typically insidious in onset, chronic, and progressive. Chronic outlet obstruction leads to urinary retention and may cause the formation of bladder diverticula or lead to hydronephrosis. Patients with urinary retention may develop urinary tract infection due to loss of hydrodynamic flushing of bacteria out of the urethra or acute kidney injury due to urinary outlet obstruction. This patient’s acute kidney injury, as evidenced by the increase in serum creatinine, is likely caused by urinary outlet obstruction secondary to BPH. Diagnosis is made by history, physical examination, and urodynamic testing, along with ruling out alternate diagnoses (eg, prostatic malignancy). The first step in diagnosis of urinary outlet obstruction is measurement of postvoid residual volume. Treatment is with supportive care, α-blockers (eg, tamsulosin), 5α-reductase inhibitors (eg, finasteride), or surgery.

wrongAnswers.B: Urine cytology (Choice B) showing malignant cells is highly specific for bladder cancer, though this finding is not always present. Cystoscopy is the gold standard for the diagnosis of bladder cancer. This patient does not have any hematuria that would be suggestive of bladder cancer, and urinary outlet obstruction is most likely due to BPH.
wrongAnswers.C: Intravenous pyelography (Choice C) involves the intravenous injection of radiopaque contrast to subsequently visualize the kidney collecting system, ureters, and bladder under fluoroscopy. This allows for the investigation of suspected urinary tract anatomic abnormalities, malignancies, and strictures. While intravenous pyelography may be helpful, it is costly and would not be the most appropriate next step, as BPH is the most likely cause of the urinary outlet obstruction, which can be illuminated by an increased postvoid residual volume.
wrongAnswers.D: Retrograde urethrography (Choice D) involves the injection of contrast into the urethra to evaluate for the extravasation of contrast, indicating urethral discontinuity. It is used to diagnose urethral injuries, which can occur from straddle injuries (anterior urethra) or pelvic fractures (posterior urethra). It is not used to diagnose chronic urinary outlet obstruction, and this patient has not sustained any urethral trauma.
wrongAnswers.E: CT scan of the abdomen (Choice E) may help diagnose other causes of urinary outlet obstruction such as nephrolithiasis or intra-abdominal tumors. This patient does not have any flank pain that would suggest nephrolithiasis or chronic abdominal pain that would suggest an intra-abdominal tumor. He has a known history of BPH, which is the most likely cause of urinary outlet obstruction. The first step in diagnosing this outlet obstruction is measurement of postvoid residual volume.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman comes to the office for a routine examination. She has osteoarthritis, hypertension, and peptic ulcer disease. Her medications are acetaminophen, lisinopril, and omeprazole. She says she has joint pain and stiffness, which limit her mobility and make it difficult for her to open her medication bottles, shop for groceries, cook, and clean. She lives alone. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows bony enlargement of the shoulders, joints of the hands, and knees. There is crepitus. Range of motion is limited by joint tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine
questions.explanation: Frailty is commonly encountered in older patients as a result of a variety of factors and presents with multiple problems across medical, functional, and social domains. In this scenario, this older patient who lives alone presents with several medical comorbidities that have resulted in difficulty performing activities of daily living. A multidisciplinary geriatrics assessment involves an evaluation by a team of several different specialists and may include physicians, occupational or physical therapists, social workers, and home health nurses or aids. A multidisciplinary assessment can help to identify the patient’s needs and goals and address medical, physical, and social challenges while coordinating an overall plan to meet these goals and to regularly assess progress. The patient in this scenario may benefit from pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment of her osteoarthritis, physical therapy to improve mobility, assessment by a home health nurse to improve her ability to function independently, as well as a social work assessment to ensure that she has adequate social support.

A multidisciplinary geriatrics assessment can help to identify her needs prior to planning for pharmacologic therapy.
wrongAnswers.B: Intra-articular administration of a corticosteroid (Choice B) is an appropriate choice for treatment of osteoarthritis, particularly of the knee or hip, that is refractory to more conservative treatment with exercise and topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. This patient’s osteoarthritis affects a variety of joints and has led to multiple problems with activities of daily living, including opening pill bottles and cooking. Injection of corticosteroids alone is both premature at this time and also unlikely to address all of her functional difficulties with activities of daily living.
wrongAnswers.D: Orthopaedic consultation (Choice D) is not necessary at this time. Osteoarthritis is best managed initially with conservative treatment including exercise and topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Refractory pain involving certain joints can be treated with intra-articular corticosteroid injections. If pain or functional limitation is refractory to these treatments, an orthopaedic consultation may be warranted to assess the need for possible joint replacement.
wrongAnswers.E: Placement in a nursing care facility (Choice E) is premature at this time. A multidisciplinary geriatrics assessment should first be performed to assess the patient’s goals and priorities in order to provide patient-centered care. If living independently is a priority, an assessment may be able to help her meet this goal and continue to live independently. Placement in a nursing care facility may be considered if those measures fail or if the patient no longer wishes to continue living independently.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-week history of mild headaches and fatigue. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not smoke cigarettes. He drinks two to three beers nightly. Four months ago, he began a highly stressful new job, in which he has a verbally abusive boss. He says he has financial concerns and is worried about job security. He used to exercise three times weekly but stopped exercising 3 months ago because he is “too busy.” He lives alone and is not in a romantic relationship. He appears tired and withdrawn and responds to questions with short phrases. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.explanation: This patient demonstrates signs of major depressive disorder (MDD), including decreased mood, fatigue, and decreased motivation (as indicated by his social withdrawal, commonly indicating anhedonia). Symptoms of MDD include 2 or more weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, and/or neurovegetative symptoms (eg, decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). By definition, these symptoms disrupt everyday functioning (eg, decreased self-care in the form of exercise). MDD commonly arises from a combination of genetic vulnerability and stressful life events, as seen with this patient. Whereas many women with MDD present with sadness, men with MDD may not present with overt sadness but may present with irritability, decreased interest in work, and fatigue. Depression in men also commonly presents with somatic symptoms. MDD and somatic symptoms (especially pain symptoms) commonly co-occur, which is postulated to arise from a common descending pain pathway. MDD is commonly treated with the combination of antidepressant medication and psychotherapy.

MDD is commonly treated with a combination of antidepressant medication and psychotherapy.

wrongAnswers.A: Alcohol use disorder (Choice A) is a clinical diagnosis made by the presence of personal, professional, social, emotional, behavioral, and physical disturbances related to the use professional, social, emotional, behavioral, and physical disturbances related to the use of alcohol or attempts to reduce intake. This patient drinks slightly more than recommended, which is likely an attempt to cope with MDD. However, his daily dysfunction is not related to excessive alcohol use or attempts to obtain more alcohol. Given his social withdrawal and pervasive fatigue, his dysfunction is instead likely related to underlying MDD.
wrongAnswers.B: Antisocial personality disorder (Choice B) is a cluster B personality disorder that arises from a deficit in empathy, resulting in pervasive violations of others’ rights, aggression, and a hostile and manipulative attitude toward others. These patients may also be chronically bored and hence sensation-seeking, leading to a high rate of substance abuse and gambling. This patient does not demonstrate aggression or a hostile attitude. His social withdrawal is more consistent with MDD.
wrongAnswers.C: Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment for longer than 6 months. This patient’s worries are specific to his work situation. Social withdrawal (indicating decreased motivation) and pervasive fatigue are more consistent with MDD.
wrongAnswers.E: Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice E) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance of trauma reminders, and/or negative mood and thoughts resulting from a traumatic event, such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, and lasting more than 1 month. This patient reports that his anxiety is specific to financial and occupational security rather than a specific traumatic event, making MDD more likely.

Cardiac stress scintigraphy showed a small area of reversible ischemia. The patient was diagnosed with stable angina; after beginning metoprolol therapy, her chest pain decreased from twice to once weekly. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications. Her temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), pulse is 62/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnormalities. Her previous physician recommended that she undergo cardiac catheterization, but she declined after researching the procedure on the Internet. She says she has read that medication alone is an acceptable alternative to cardiac catheterization and that she is unwilling to accept the risks associated with the procedure. She agrees to add atorvastatin to her medication regimen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Obstetrics
questions.explanation: Clinicians should maintain a low threshold of suspicion for pregnancy in reproductive-age patients presenting with changes in their menstrual cycles, especially when those patients use contraception inconsistently. Early symptoms of pregnancy in addition to irregular menstruation include fatigue, nausea, breast tenderness, and urinary frequency. While amenorrhea is a more common sign of early pregnancy, light vaginal bleeding can occur with the implantation of a fertilized ovum and can be misinterpreted as a menstrual cycle. Evaluation of these patients includes measurement of β-hCG concentration in the urine or serum, with the concentration being increased in pregnant patients. Transvaginal ultrasonography can be used to confirm the diagnosis. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis in this patient presenting with nausea and changes in her menstrual cycle is thus measurement of urine β-hCG concentration.

His diabetes mellitus has been fairly well controlled with metformin. At his last visit 3 months ago, his hemoglobin A1c was 7.8%, and his metformin was increased from 850 mg twice daily to 1000 mg twice daily. He also takes glipizide and atorvastatin. Laboratory studies, including a complete metabolic panel, serum lipid studies, and screening of the urine for microalbumin done during the previous visit 3 months ago, were all within the reference ranges. questions.subject: Endocrinology
questions.explanation: The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends various screening tests and interventions for patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus should be screened for high blood pressure at every medical visit. Lipid profile screening should be done at least every 5 years to measure total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides. An annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio test and blood test to measure serum creatinine should be performed to detect early-stage kidney damage. Comprehensive eye examination, foot examination, depression screening, weight management counseling, and tobacco cessation counseling are also recommended annually. However, guidelines may need to be individualized based on a patient's specific clinical characteristics and comorbidities. Given that this patient has had all the above studies except for a foot examination at the visit 3 months prior, this is the most appropriate step at this time.

She is at the 75th percentile for length and 50th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 38.3°C (101°F). Examination shows purulent nasal drainage. questions.subject: Otolaryngology
questions.explanation: Acute otitis media is an acute infection of the middle ear and usually spreads to this space via the Eustachian (auditory) tubes from the nasopharynx. The middle ear is bounded externally by the tympanic membrane and internally by the oval window. The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the posterior aspect of the nasopharynx near the torus tubarius. Acute otitis media classically occurs in infants and children, often from viral or bacterial pathogens, commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae or Haemophilus influenzae. It presents with ear pain, often with fever, and an erythematous tympanic membrane with retrotympanic pus or a middle ear effusion, as in this case. Infants may present with nonspecific signs of fussiness, decreased appetite, and poor sleeping, as well as ear tugging. Recurrent episodes may lead to mastoiditis or scarring of the tympanic membrane with associated conductive hearing loss. First-line therapy includes antibiotic treatment with amoxicillin with or without clavulanate, as well as symptomatic treatment. Amoxicillin is a β-lactam antibiotic with broad activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae; it is commonly used to treat pediatric upper respiratory tract, sinus, and ear infections.

Growth and development have been normal. His medical records indicate that vaccinations were up-to-date through age 9 years; he has not received any vaccinations since that time. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Administration of which of the following vaccines is most appropriate at this time?

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine
questions.explanation: This patient would benefit from vaccination with meningococcal vaccine, protecting him against infection by Neisseria meningitidis, which may lead to life-threatening meningitis or sepsis. Meningococcal disease is more prevalent in low- and middle-income countries, but it may occur in the United States in crowded conditions, such as dormitories, barracks, or prisons. Meningococcal vaccine is available as a conjugate vaccine and a recombinant protein serogroup B vaccine. The conjugate vaccine is indicated for all children and is administered in two doses, the first at age 11 to 12 years and the second at age 16 years. The serogroup B vaccine is given as an additional dose, usually between age 16 and 18 years, particularly in teens who plan to attend an institution of higher education or enlist in the military. Certain teenage patients at particular risk for infection with N. meningitidis or other encapsulated organisms, such as patients with functional or anatomic asplenia or complement deficiency, should receive vaccination with serogroup B vaccine regardless of their plans to attend college or university.

This patient has likely already received two doses of measles-mumps-rubella vaccine.
wrongAnswers.E: Pneumococcal vaccine (Choice E), available as either a 13-valent or 15-valent conjugate vaccine, is indicated for all children to prevent infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae. The 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine is indicated for all adults over age 65 years and in patients with high-risk conditions, such as chronic heart, kidney, and liver disease or chronic smokers. This patient has likely already received four doses of pneumococcal vaccine and does not require additional pneumococcal vaccination at this time.

questions.subject: Gastroenterology
questions.explanation: Increased liver enzymes are often identified in asymptomatic patients. These increases in liver enzymes can be classified into different patterns. A hepatocellular pattern is when there is a greater increase in aminotransferases compared with alkaline phosphatase. A cholestatic pattern is when there is a greater increase in alkaline phosphatase compared with aminotransferases. questions.subject: Endocrinology
questions.explanation: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in high-resource nations and occurs due to the presence of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor-stimulating antibodies. This results in a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland on physical examination, which can cause signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, diaphoresis, and pretibial myxedema, though some patients (such as the one in this case) may be clinically asymptomatic. TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies also stimulate orbital fibroblasts and can lead to thyroid ophthalmopathy, which is characterized by the expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue with resultant exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus. Thyroid function testing typically shows increased concentrations of T3 and T4, and decreased TSH. Additional testing for TSH-receptor stimulating antibodies confirms the diagnosis. Radioactive iodine uptake nuclear scintigraphy typically shows diffuse, abnormally increased uptake of the thyroid gland without a discrete nodule. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs, radioiodine ablation, and surgery.

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine
questions.explanation:
Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for coronary artery disease, the most common cause of mortality in adults. The Framingham Heart Study found that smoking is associated with an approximately two-fold increase in morbidity and mortality from ischemic heart disease. Smoking is also associated with various cancers, stroke, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which are also associated with increased mortality rates. Smoking can exacerbate type 2 diabetes mellitus. Therefore, for this patient and most patients, smoking cessation is the most beneficial behavior change. Patients should be advised that it is never too late to stop smoking, as the increased cardiovascular risk and other risks associated with smoking begins to decline immediately upon smoking cessation. motivation to change, is helpful when discussing health behavior changes, such as smoking cessation, with patients.

questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics
questions.explanation:
Osteoarthritis is a noninflammatory arthropathy that occurs secondary to deterioration of articular cartilage. It typically occurs in older patients and may affect any joint. The hips and knees are commonly affected because of chronic weight bearing, with the shoulders and hands also being commonly affected joints. Osteoarthritis is not associated with infectious or inflammatory symptoms and is generally insidious in onset. Patients typically complain of chronic pain in a joint that is worse with movement or exertion and is improved with rest. Patients often have limited range of motion caused by underlying joint space narrowing and pain. Imaging may show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral cysts, or sclerotic changes, as seen in this patient’s shoulder x-ray. First-line treatment is conservative with physical therapy and oral pain medications as needed. Initial pharmacologic options include acetaminophen, although only a minority of patients will achieve meaningful relief with this therapy alone. Additional options include

nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications, intra-articular injections (eg, cortisone), and joint replacement surgery for severe or refractory cases. In this case, the patient has cardiac and kidney disease, which is a contraindication to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications as they have been shown to increase the risk for myocardial infarction and kidney injury. The most appropriate next step in management for this patient is physical therapy.

questions.subject: Nephrology/Urology
questions.explanation: This patient has a presentation consistent with acute epididymitis, and the most appropriate next step in management is antibiotic therapy. Acute epididymitis, or infection of the epididymis, most commonly presents with unilateral scrotal pain associated with a tender, swollen mass over the posterior aspect of the testis. In severe cases, such as this patient’s, it can also present with localized erythema, dysuria, and systemic symptoms such as fever and rigors. Physical examination will show an intact cremasteric reflex, which helps differentiate acute epididymitis from testicular torsion, in which the cremasteric reflex is often absent. The underlying cause is most commonly infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in men under age 35 years, whereas Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas species are the more common causative organisms in older men or in men having unprotected insertive anal intercourse. Evaluation should include urine nucleic acid amplification testing for both C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae, as well as urinalysis and urine culture. Treatment includes empiric ceftriaxone to cover gonorrheal infection and doxycycline or azithromycin to cover chlamydial infection in patients at risk for sexually transmitted infections. Levofloxacin or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are the recommended agents for patients at low risk for sexually transmitted infections. Symptomatic management includes scrotal elevation, application of ice, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

questions.subject: Biostatistics/Epidemiology
questions.explanation: A randomized trial is a stringent type of prospective study wherein patients are randomly assigned to receive a particular intervention. The intervention may be compared against placebo therapy or against standard therapy. Randomized control studies form the gold standard of medical research and generate strong evidence as compared to observational or descriptive studies. For any study to be valid, regardless of design, internal and external validity must be considered. Internal validity describes the degree to which a study establishes or supports a faithful conclusion about cause and effect (whether the design of the study was sufficient to support the conclusion drawn). Sufficient internal validity should limit the degree to which alternative explanations of cause and effect can be reasonably drawn. Internal validity thus refers to whether the exposure, treatment, or variable being tested makes a difference, and whether the experiment was designed in a way to support the claim. External validity determines whether an experiment can be generalized, and its conclusions applied to groups beyond those considered in the study population. In this example, the sample comprises a specific demographic group: young women with streptococcal pharyngitis. The restricted range of demographic characteristics decreases the likelihood of confounding variables. The external validity is decreased compared to the internal validity of this study.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common form of skin cancer, following basal cell carcinoma. SCC of the skin is related to chronic UV damage, which triggers the development of thymidine dimers and mutations in p53, a tumor suppressor gene. Additional risk factors involved in the development of SCC include iatrogenic immunosuppression, especially in solid organ transplant patients, and genetic diseases, including albinism and xeroderma pigmentosum. SCC classically presents as a rough papule or nodule with erosion or ulceration and overlying hyperkeratotic scale. Pathology discloses parakeratosis, loss of the epidermal granular layer, full-thickness epidermal atypia, keratin pearls, and invasion into the dermis. Unlike basal cell carcinoma, SCC carries a higher risk for metastasis, especially in lesions with neurovascular involvement. Lesions consistent with SCC warrant skin biopsy and are treated with excision-based therapies, including Mohs micrographic surgery or electrodessication and curettage. This patient’s chronic, eroded, scaly lesion on sun-exposed skin is suggestive of SCC.

His birth weight was 3500 g (7 lb 11 oz) and his current weight is 7000 g (15 lb 7 oz). The parents ask if their child's weight gain is appropriate. His weight gain is too rapid for his age
questions.subject: Pediatrics/Neonatology
questions.explanation:
Growth rates are a useful way of assessing a child’s growth over a given interval of time and can detect abnormal growth patterns that may indicate underlying medical conditions. There are several frequently employed growth charts, including the chart shown, which was developed by the National Center for Health Statistics, as well as charts from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health

Organization. Growth charts plot the expected length and weight of a child of a particular sex at a given age. Percentiles are also plotted for length and weight at a particular age. In this scenario, the patient was born at 3500 g (7 lb 11 oz), which falls near the 50th percentile for birth weight. At age 4 months, he weighs 7000 g (15 lb 7 oz), which falls near the 65th percentile of weight for his age. The parents should be reassured that this weight gain is appropriate. Children at extreme ends of the growth curves are often healthy. However, persistent accelerated or decelerated growth rates usually warrant further investigation. Common causes of accelerated weight gain include endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypercortisolism) or genetic abnormalities (eg, Down syndrome), while decelerated weight gain may occur because of malnutrition, immunodeficiency, or metabolic or organ system abnormalities. Accelerated length gain may occur as a result of metabolic or genetic abnormalities, such as Marfan syndrome, seminiferous tubule dysgenesis (Klinefelter syndrome), or homocystinuria, or excess of growth hormone, while decelerated length gain may occur because of growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, anemia, or organ system abnormalities. Both height and weight percentiles and growth rates should be considered when any abnormality is suspected.

questions.explanation:
Thalassemia is the most likely diagnosis in this postmenopausal patient with mild microcytic anemia and a normal ferritin concentration presenting with 2 months of progressive fatigue. Thalassemia is an inherited condition in which one or more alleles of either the α- or β-globin genes is rendered nonfunctional, thereby interfering with normal synthesis of hemoglobin A (HbA). Normal adult hemoglobin consists of two α-globin subunits and two β-globin subunits, which together form α2β2 (HbA), a unique conformation that has a high affinity for oxygen in the lungs and can offload oxygen effectively in the peripheral tissues. In patients who have one or more deficient β-globin genes (β-thalassemia major or minor), the normal HbA molecule cannot be effectively assembled, and the excess α-globin chains combine with one another to form insoluble tetramers. There are four α-globin alleles, and the severity of α-thalassemia depends upon the number of these alleles that are nonfunctional. Many patients with α-thalassemia trait are asymptomatic and only exhibit minimal decreases in hemoglobin concentration, although microcytosis is frequently encountered. Patients with more nonfunctional alleles present with increasingly severe levels of anemia Microcytosis and

nonfunctional alleles present with increasingly severe levels of anemia. Microcytosis and the presence of target cells on peripheral blood smear are characteristic of both α- and β-thalassemia. These two conditions can be reliably distinguished using hemoglobin electrophoresis. Patients with thalassemia trait or thalassemia minor are often incorrectly diagnosed as having iron deficiency anemia, and in these instances, oral iron therapy will have no effect on the hemoglobin concentration. This patient’s normal ferritin concentration helps exclude iron deficiency as the cause.

Hemoglobin electrophoresis can be used to distinguish between these two entities. Treatment is often not necessary.

questions.explanation: Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is characterized as the presence of a blood clot within a deep vein of the upper or lower extremities and is a common issue in patients who spend prolonged time sitting (such as the bus driver in this example). The formation of a DVT is promoted by features of Virchow triad: venous stasis (eg, immobility, venous occlusion), endothelial injury (eg, infection, trauma, inflammation, cannulation), and hypercoagulability (eg, malignancy, genetic or acquired thrombophilia). A patient with a history of consistent immobility and new unilateral extremity swelling should undergo duplex ultrasonography of the extremity to evaluate for the presence of DVT. There are both modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors associated with venous thromboembolic disease. Modifiable actions to reduce the incidence of DVT include minimizing immobility, especially in the prothrombotic postoperative state, avoiding hormonal birth control, smoking cessation, weight loss, and, if immobilized, using a prophylactic anticoagulant such as low-dose subcutaneous heparin. Nonmodifiable risk factors include age, history of genetic or acquired hypercoagulability, family history, and pregnancy. Complications of DVT include embolus to the lung, phlegmasia cerulea or alba dolens, and post-thrombotic syndrome. Treatment includes anticoagulation, placement of inferior vena cava filters, thrombolysis, or thrombectomy.

questions.subject: Infectious Disease
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing mycobacterial organism transmitted via respiratory secretions. It presents with primary, latent, and reactivation patterns. Tuberculosis is more common and spreads more easily in crowded populations, such as in nursing facilities and prisons. In primary disease, patients have a history of subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. Latent tuberculosis can occur as the organism proliferates within macrophages and is maintained within caseating granulomas. Purified protein derivative (PPD) skin testing, also known as tuberculin skin testing (TST), stimulates a T lymphocyte-driven type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction against subdermal tuberculin antigen. Causes of false-positive results include prior vaccination with BCG vaccine. A positive result such as in this patient with no evidence of active tuberculosis (normal chest x-ray and sputum Gram stain) is diagnostic of latent tuberculosis infection. Latent tuberculosis is treated with a prolonged course of isoniazid or rifampin. The most recent guidelines recommend a course of rifamycin-based monotherapy.

questions.subject: Gastroenterology
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is a gluten-sensitive enteropathy that is mediated through immune intolerance of the protein gliadin, commonly found in wheat products. This results in inflammatory infiltration of the proximal small bowel, which leads to characteristic intraepithelial lymphocytosis, villous atrophy, and crypt hyperplasia. Malabsorption of substances in the proximal small bowel ensues, which presents symptomatically as chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and nutritional deficiencies. Patients with celiac disease may develop iron deficiency anemia, which may be present on laboratory studies with decreased hematocrit and microcytosis. The diagnosis of celiac disease can be confirmed by the detection of serum antitransglutaminase antibodies or by small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy along with intraepithelial lymphocytes and crypt hyperplasia. Treatment includes avoidance of gluten-containing foods and reversal of any acquired nutritional deficiencies. This patient with a 3-year history of abdominal discomfort improved by elimination of wheat products likely has underlying celiac disease, characterized by villous atrophy identified on small bowel biopsy.

Although this patient does have weight loss and mild anxiety, celiac disease is more likely in the setting of improved symptoms after eliminating wheat products from her diet.

A patient with improving abdominal symptoms after eliminating wheat products from their diet most likely has celiac disease.
wrongAnswers.C: Transmural intestinal inflammation (Choice C) is a finding in Crohn disease. Severe Crohn disease can result in intestinal obstruction from stricture or inflammation, bowel perforation, intra-abdominal abscesses, and the formation of fistulas. wrongAnswers.D: Ulceration of colonic mucosa (Choice D) is a finding of ulcerative colitis. Ulcerative colitis is a type of inflammatory bowel disease that results in mucosal and submucosal ulceration and inflammation that progresses retrograde from the rectum to the colon. This typically presents with chronic bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and abdominal pain. Because of the improving symptoms after elimination of wheat from this patient's diet, celiac disease is more likely.

questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences
questions.explanation: Physicians should deliver bad news in a thoughtful and patient-centered manner. Prior to delivering bad news, physicians should first attempt to clarify patients’ preferences for delivery of the news. These questions should inquire about how much and what type of information a patient desires to hear. Information about a poor prognosis commonly changes a patient’s life, and some patients may prefer not to know all of the details of their prognosis. The physician should deliver news according to the patient’s preferences. This patient-centered approach honors patient autonomy.

questions.subject: Preventive Medicine
questions.explanation: Pneumococcal vaccine, available as either a 13-valent or 15-valent conjugate vaccine or as a 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine, protects against infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae. The conjugate vaccine is typically given as four doses at ages 2, 4, 6 months, and between ages 12 and 15 months. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices recommends routine vaccination for protection against pneumococcal disease for infants, children, and adults 65 years of age or older. Pneumococcal disease is responsible for a large burden of morbidity and mortality, and large-scale vaccination programs have been effective in reducing the burden of disease. It is recommended that this patient receive the pneumococcal 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) at this time because of his history of cirrhosis, which increases his risk for developing pneumococcal disease. Adults over age 65 years who do not have an immunocompromising condition (including cirrhosis), cerebrospinal fluid leak, or cochlear implant should receive one dose of PPSV23. Any patients who received PPSV23 prior to turning age 65 years should receive a single additional dose after age 65 years and at least 5 years after the prior dose.

questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by diffusely low bone density. Evaluation for osteoporosis involves a DEXA scan and is defined as a bone mineral density less than 2.5 standard deviations compared to a young, normal population (T-score). The United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends, at the Grade B level, to screen women over age 65 years for osteoporosis, and under age 65 years when increased risk factors exist. The most common risk factors for the development of osteoporosis are age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women. Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic but increases the risk for fractures, most commonly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Calcium and vitamin D supplementations are recommended for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. Recommendation should be made for weight-bearing exercise in the absence of other contraindications to slow deterioration of bone mineral density. Bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast activity and can be used to treat osteoporosis to reduce further loss of bone mineral density. For this 66-year-old patient, a DEXA scan is the most appropriate screening test at this time.

questions.subject: Musculoskeletal/Orthopedics
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disease characterized by diffusely low bone density. Evaluation for osteoporosis involves a DEXA scan and is defined as a bone mineral density less than 2.5 standard deviations compared to a young, normal population (T-score). The most common risk factors for the development of osteoporosis are age, smoking, chronic inflammatory disease, corticosteroid use, and estrogen-depleting conditions in women. Osteoporosis is often asymptomatic but increases the risk for fractures, most commonly involving the hip, vertebrae, and distal radius. Calcium and vitamin D supplementations are recommended for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. In addition to vitamin supplementation, bisphosphonates, such as alendronate, are typically the first-line medications used in osteoporosis to reduce further loss of bone density by binding to hydroxyapatite on bony surfaces to inhibit osteoclastic bone resorption. This patient has a T-score of -2.8, making osteoporosis the most likely diagnosis. Alendronate therapy is the most appropriate next step in treatment.

Alendronate is the next best step in management of this patient newly diagnosed with osteoporosis without contraindications to bisphosphonate therapy.

wrongAnswers.B: Atorvastatin therapy (Choice B) is generally recommended for patients with a 10-year arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk less than 10%. For a patient newly diagnosed with osteoporosis and no contraindications to bisphosphonates, alendronate therapy is the most appropriate next step in management.
wrongAnswers.D: Omega-3 fish oil supplementation (Choice D) may be considered for patients with conditions such as hypertriglyceridemia. wrongAnswers.E: Raloxifene therapy (Choice E) may be a reasonable treatment option for a patient diagnosed with osteoporosis who is unable to tolerate bisphosphonate therapy. However, raloxifene has been shown to decrease the risk for developing breast cancer. questions.stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of shortness of breath with exertion. He also has had paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and orthopnea. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease; he had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. Current medications include simvastatin and aspirin. His pulse is 100/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Crackles are heard on auscultation. There is an S3. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly, cephalization of blood flow, and Kerley B lines. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to improve this patient's chances of survival?

questions.subject: Cardiology
questions.explanation: This patient with dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 heart sound has a presentation consistent with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). Patients with decompensated heart failure may additionally present with jugular venous distention and peripheral edema on physical exam. Chest x-ray may show pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Laboratory studies often show an increased brain natriuretic peptide concentration. Echocardiogram is the gold standard for diagnosis and may show either reduced ejection fraction or preserved ejection fraction with diastolic heart failure. There are numerous causes of heart failure, including ischemic heart disease, hypertension, valvulopathy, pulmonary disease, infection, arrhythmias, and congenital causes. Treatment of heart failure involves the management of underlying causes and associated conditions, as well as appropriate pharmacotherapy to improve symptoms, preserve myocardial function, and reduce mortality. Initial guideline-recommended therapy is a combination of a β-adrenergic blocking agent, a renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitor, and a diuretic. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, as well as β-adrenergic blocking agents, aldosterone receptor blockers (ARB), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists have been shown to reduce mortality in patients with heart failure.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man comes to the office because of a 5-year history of slowly worsening constipation. During this time, his stools have been hard and have decreased in frequency. He reports often having to strain and a sensation of incomplete evacuation following bowel movements. This is the first time he has sought treatment. Colonoscopy 5 years ago showed no abnormalities. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes hydrochlorothiazide. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination discloses a palpable colon with hard stool over the left of the abdomen; the remainder of the physical examination shows no other abnormalities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. In addition to increasing fluid intake, which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy?

questions.subject: Gastroenterology
questions.explanation: Constipation is a common condition that can develop idiopathically or secondary to many different causes, including metabolic derangements, medication adverse effects, hypothyroidism, spinal cord injury, and pregnancy. Initial management of idiopathic constipation includes patient education, dietary changes such as increasing water and fiber intake, as well as bulking or non-bulking laxatives. Psyllium is an example of a bulk-forming laxative that helps to increase stool frequency, as well as soften stool as a result of its fiber content. If increased fiber does not control the constipation, many other stool medications are available such as sennosides, polyethylene glycol, lactulose, docusate sodium, and magnesium citrate. For this patient seeking first-time treatment who does not have a clear secondary cause to his constipation, psyllium is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy.

Psyllium is a source of fiber and an example of a bulk-forming laxative that helps to increase stool frequency as well as soften stool. In this case of previously untreated constipation, psyllium is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy.

wrongAnswers.A: Lactulose (Choice A) is an osmotic laxative that functions to increase the water content inside the colon and stool. Lactulose is also used in cases of hepatic encephalopathy to decrease the intestinal production and absorption of ammonia. In this case of a patient seeking first-time treatment with presumed idiopathic constipation, psyllium is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy.
wrongAnswers.B: Linaclotide (Choice B) is a medication used to treat chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome. Linaclotide functions by increasing intestinal secretions through the induction of cyclic guanosine monophosphate, which results in increased chloride and bicarbonate and thus higher fluid content in the intestinal lumen. In this case of previously untreated, presumed idiopathic constipation, the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy is psyllium.
wrongAnswers.C: Lubiprostone (Choice C) is a medication to treat chronic idiopathic constipation and irritable bowel syndrome. Lubiprostone functions by activating a chloride channel along the intestine to increase intestinal fluid secretion. The most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy in this case of previously untreated, presumed idiopathic constipation is psyllium.
wrongAnswers.D: Magnesium citrate (Choice D) is an osmotic laxative. Magnesium citrate functions by increasing the intraluminal water content, causing colonic distension and resultant colonic peristalsis. Magnesium citrate can be a reasonable option for cases of constipation but is only recommended for occasional use. In this case of constipation without prior treatment, psyllium is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy.

His father had prostate cancer at the age of 85 years. Examination of the patient shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding prostate cancer screening for this patient?

His father had prostate cancer at the age of 85 years. Examination of the patient shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step regarding prostate cancer screening for this patient?
choices: Digital rectal examination and measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) concentration
Discussing the risks and benefits of prostate cancer screening options and allowing the patient to decide
Measurement of serum PSA concentration only
Prostate cancer screening is not indicated for this patient
questions.subject: Preventive Medicine
questions.explanation: The most appropriate next step for this patient is discussing the risks and benefits of prostate cancer screening options and allowing the patient to decide. Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men. It is commonly asymptomatic but can present with urinary symptoms, such as urinary hesitancy or hematuria, or bone pain if metastatic. Risk factors for its development include advancing age, certain ethnicities and geographic locations, family history of prostate cancer, and certain genetic factors (eg, BRCA mutations, Lynch syndrome). While screening patients over age 55 years with measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) concentrations may decrease the risk of death from prostate cancer, there are significant risks and harms associated with screening, such as false-positive test results that lead to additional testing or the need for biopsy. As many prostate cancers remain indolent and do not become clinically significant prior to a patient’s death, even appropriate diagnosis of prostate cancer with a screening test can be associated with harms, such as those associated with surgical resection and chemoradiotherapy. As such, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends that the decision to screen for prostate cancer between ages 55 and 69 years be an individual decision made by a patient based on their health values after engaging in shared decision-making with their physician. The USPSTF does not recommend screening for patients over age 70 years.
questions.educationalObjective: Prostate cancer is a common cause of malignancy in men. While screening patients over age 55 years with measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentrations may decrease the risk of death from prostate cancer, there are significant risks and harms associated with screening. Given that many prostate cancers would otherwise remain indolent and not affect a patient’s overall life expectancy, the appropriate diagnosis of clinically asymptomatic prostate cancer also carries the risks associated with treatment that may have been unnecessary. As such, the United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends that the decision to screen for prostate cancer between ages 55 and 69 years be an individual decision made by a patient based on their health values after engaging in shared decision-making with their physician.

wrongAnswers.B: Digital rectal examination only (Choice B) is not recommended as an initial screening tool for prostate cancer given its low sensitivity and specificity. If the patient decides to undergo prostate cancer screening, measurement of serum PSA concentration would be the most appropriate next step.

The decision to screen for prostate cancer is an individual one and should be made by a patient based on their goals and values after discussing the risks and benefits with their provider. This patient desires prostate cancer screening, and it would be inappropriate to deny it to him.

Eighteen months ago, he had progressive difficulty reading and “seeing small things.” His symptoms initially improved with the use of weak reading glasses; he then required stronger reading glasses. He reports no other current problems with his vision and is otherwise asymptomatic. He has hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide. Vital signs are within normal limits. Visual acuity is 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right eye. No other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.explanation: This middle-aged patient who presents with progressive difficulty with near vision somewhat improved with weak reading glasses is likely experiencing presbyopia, an age-related loss of the eye’s accommodative ability. Accommodation describes the ability of the eye to alter/increase its refractive power in order to focus on near visual targets. The Helmholtz theory of accommodation holds that contraction of the ciliary muscle relaxes tension of the zonular fibers upon the crystalline lens, allowing the lens to become rounder, thereby increasing the curvature of its anterior surface and increasing its dioptric power, allowing for focusing on objects at close distances. The accommodative ability of the lens is dependent upon its ability to distend its shape. Presbyopia is a normal age-related change. Patients present with blurry vision at near-distance and notice that objects must be held at farther working distances to be seen clearly. Normal pupillary reflexes to accommodation are not affected by presbyopia. Treatment is with reading glasses with positive dioptric power. This patient is currently maintaining good visual acuity and is doing well with stronger reading glasses, so no further management is indicated at this time.

wrongAnswers.A: Glaucoma screening (Choice A) is incorrect. Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy that results in loss of retinal ganglion cell axons and loss of peripheral vision. Its course is typically insidious and chronic. The hallmark of glaucoma is cupping of the optic disc. While patients with glaucoma may maintain excellent visual acuity until late stages of disease, glaucoma does not typically present with loss of accommodative ability or difficulties with near vision, which are more suggestive of presbyopia.
wrongAnswers.B: Measurement of fasting serum glucose concentration (Choice B) is useful for the diagnosis of diabetes. While diabetes may result in symptoms of blurry vision, visual distortion, or frank vision loss as a result of diabetic retinopathy or diabetic macular edema, it does not result in loss of near vision while sparing distance vision.
wrongAnswers.C: Referral to an ophthalmologist (Choice C) is not necessary at this time. This patient is seeing well with reading glasses and maintaining good visual acuity. A referral to ophthalmology may be warranted if the patient was unhappy with his vision or if his visual acuity was below 20/40, at which an evaluation for cataract, refractive error, or other causes of vision loss would be warranted.
wrongAnswers.D: Ultrasonography of the carotid arteries (Choice D) is useful for the diagnosis of amaurosis fugax or branch retinal artery occlusion, which may result in cholesterol embolization to the retinal vasculature. Amaurosis fugax presents with brief episodes of transient, unilateral, painless vision loss as a result of microembolization of the ophthalmic artery, while branch retinal artery occlusion presents with sudden, often sectoral vision loss that does not fluctuate. Patients with amaurosis fugax or branch retinal artery occlusion should be treated similarly to acute ischemic stroke with emergent systemic evaluation. Neither condition presents with isolated loss of near vision, as in this scenario.

questions.subject: Pulmonology
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that results from inhalation of asbestos fibers, leading to progressive inflammation and fibrosis of the alveoli and pulmonary interstitium. Patients may be asymptomatic or may develop chronic pulmonary disease characterized by a chronic cough and dyspnea associated with progressive pulmonary fibrosis. Occupational exposure is the greatest risk factor for developing asbestosis. Occupations with notable risk for asbestos exposure include plumbers, pipefitters, steamfitters, electricians, insulation workers, carpenters, general laborers, boilermakers, welders, cutters, and janitors. Physical examination may disclose pulmonary crackles, digital clubbing, and signs of pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy such as a parasternal heave, loud P2, and widely split S2. Characteristic imaging findings may include bilateral infiltrates with a lower lung predominance, calcified pleural plaques, and rounded atelectasis. Pleural effusions may be present.

questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences
questions.explanation: Arranging for telephone (or in-person, if available) interpreter services should be the physician’s first step. Professional interpreters can provide high-quality translations that maintain patient safety. Credentialed interpreters are trained in medical knowledge and vocabulary, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. Relying on a family member for interpreting increases the risk for miscommunication about medical or culturally relevant details and can jeopardize informed consent for treatment and patient safety. This is important for all care, but particularly so in this case as a miscommunication through the patient’s daughter could lead to blood pressure mismanagement and hypertensive urgency.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.explanation: A thorough substance use history is needed in patients who are experiencing psychological distress (eg, in the setting of a stressor) or who carry psychiatric diagnoses, as substance use is commonly comorbid in these populations. Patients may cope with stress by using internal or external strategies, which may be adaptive or maladaptive. An example of an adaptive internal coping strategy is cognitive reframing or viewing the situation in a different way. An example of a maladaptive external coping strategy is using substances to numb or avoid emotions. This patient is experiencing distress and demonstrates fatigue, anhedonia, and decreased appetite in the setting of a stressor, meeting criteria for adjustment disorder. Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. As such, the physician should screen him for alcohol and drug use disorder. The treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy to support adaptive coping.

questions.subject: Cardiology
questions.explanation: Endocarditis prophylaxis is recommended for patients with high-risk cardiac features undergoing procedures that put them at increased risk for the development of bacterial endocarditis. These cardiac features include prosthetic heart valves, prior infective endocarditis, unrepaired congenital cyanotic heart disease or repaired disease with residual shunts or valvular regurgitation near prosthetic material, repaired congenital defects with a catheter-based intervention (for the first six months after the procedure), and valvular regurgitation in a heart transplant recipient. High-risk procedures include dental procedures with gingival manipulation or perforation of the oral mucosa, respiratory tract procedures in which the mucosa is violated, procedures on infected soft tissue, and cardiac surgery with prosthetic material. This patient’s cardiac features do not indicate the need for prophylaxis before dental cleaning.
questions.educationalObjective: Patients with unrepaired congenital cyanotic heart disease, a prior history of endocarditis, or those with prosthetic valves should receive antibiotic prophylaxis against endocarditis prior to invasive dental or respiratory tract procedures. The treatment of choice is typically amoxicillin. In patients with a penicillin allergy, a macrolide is the preferred agent. Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to dental cleaning is not indicated for patients lacking these cardiac features.

questions.subject: Obstetrics
questions.explanation:
Pregnancy is suspected when there is a missed or delayed menstrual period. An ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in the fallopian tube (most common), on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or in any nonendometrial location. A history of pelvic inflammatory disease is an important risk factor. Ectopic pregnancy often presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominopelvic pain. β-hCG concentrations will be increased, leading to positive urine and serum pregnancy tests. Ectopic pregnancies are nonviable. Diagnosis can often be confirmed with transvaginal ultrasonography, which would fail to show an intrauterine gestational sac. Transvaginal ultrasonography is the most appropriate next step for this patient. Ectopic pregnancies can be managed medically, using methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, but may require salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy for larger pregnancies, in cases of medical treatment failure, or in any case of complication. One complication of an unrecognized ectopic pregnancy is rupture, leading to bleeding and hemoperitoneum. In this instance, physical examination may show abdominal guarding. Severe cases may lead to hemorrhagic shock, with tachycardia, hypotension, and anemia. Treatment of a

ruptured ectopic pregnancy is emergent exploratory laparotomy.

questions.explanation: Hyponatremia has many causes, including but not limited to excessive fluid intake, diuretic use, adrenal insufficiency, heart failure, and kidney disease. In the case of this patient, while running a marathon and sweating profusely, he replenished his fluids with free water only, which is hypotonic to the sweat that was lost. Because of this, the patient had a progressive and relatively rapid decline in his overall sodium concentration resulting in symptomatic hyponatremia. As seen with this patient, symptoms include nausea, headache, vomiting, confusion, and in severe cases, potentially seizures or coma. questions.subject: Hematology/Oncology
questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia is characterized by a low platelet count, which can result in excessive bleeding and bruising. The most common causes of thrombocytopenia include immune-mediated destruction of platelets, decreased platelet production, and increased platelet consumption. In terms of immune-mediated destruction, conditions such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and drug-induced thrombocytopenia can cause platelet destruction, whereas conditions such as aplastic anemia and leukemia can lead to a decrease in platelet production. Increased platelet consumption can occur in conditions such as disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. In this patient, with no medical history and using no medications, ITP is most likely. For patients with ITP and stable platelet counts above 50,000/mm³, no interventions for thrombocytopenia are required as these patients generally do not have issues with hemostasis during dental procedures.

questions.subject: Emergency/Critical Care
questions.explanation: This patient’s presentation and findings are suggestive of acute pulmonary embolism (PE). Patients classically present with acute chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypoxemia. Some patients may also experience unexplained syncope. It is often difficult to distinguish PE from other acute respiratory disorders, and the differential includes asthma exacerbation, vocal cord dysfunction, acute coronary syndrome, panic episode, and vasovagal syncope, among others. The clinician must maintain a high index of suspicion, and the use of clinical decision aids (eg, Wells criteria) is recommended. Risk factors for acute PE include immobility, obesity, recent surgery, malignancy, pregnancy, use of oral contraceptives, trauma, fracture of long bones, and inherited thrombophilia. ECG often shows a normal sinus rhythm or sinus tachycardia. Arterial blood gas analysis typically shows acute respiratory alkalosis, hypoxemia, and an increased A-a gradient as a result of ventilation-perfusion mismatch. CT pulmonary angiography is the preferred method to confirm diagnosis.

questions.subject: Ethics/Social Sciences
questions.explanation: To protect patients’ well-being, physicians have an obligation to investigate evidence of abuse. Physicians should first ask direct, open-ended questions about physical examination findings indicative of abuse. The physician should ideally ask these questions to the patient privately, without caregivers present. If the patient denies abuse but the physician possesses enough objective evidence of abuse, the physician should proceed under the assumption that the patient is being abused and report the abuse to the appropriate authority (in this case of an elderly adult, senior protective services). Physicians are mandated by many states to report abuse of children and vulnerable adults to protective agencies. The protective agencies then investigate whether abuse has occurred and may remove vulnerable adults from dangerous situations. Physicians should treat the immediate symptoms, which may manifest as medical or psychiatric symptoms, and continue to provide regular care to monitor for long-term consequences of abuse.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.explanation: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) presents with chronic symptoms of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and/or inattention that occur in more than one setting and impair academic, social, and/or emotional function. Children with predominant hyperactivity symptoms are fidgety and may have difficulty taking turns (postulated to result from a dysregulated dopamine reward pathway), whereas children with predominant inattentive symptoms tend to daydream, process information slowly, and have difficulty completing tasks (related to norepinephrine dysregulation). For diagnosis, physicians must establish that the patient is functionally impaired in several settings, so parents and teachers must fill out behavioral rating scales. Stimulants, which include amphetamine salts and methylphenidate, are first-line treatments for children aged 6 years and older. For children younger than age 6 years, first-line treatment is parent training in behavior management, and stimulants are second-line treatment.

questions.subject: Cardiology
questions.explanation: This patient presents with acute rheumatic fever, characterized by arthritis and mitral regurgitation, following an episode of streptococcal pharyngitis. Rheumatic fever is a sequela of untreated Group A Streptococcus infection, commonly pharyngitis, in which there is a type II (complement-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction to self-antigens having a similar structure to, and thus molecularly mimicking, streptococcal M protein. Diagnosis is made using the Jones criteria, which describes many of the core clinical features of rheumatic fever. This includes the major criteria of polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, and Sydenham chorea, and the minor criteria of fever, leukocytosis, arthralgia, and PR interval prolongation. Patients often have an increased antistreptolysin O titer. Biopsy of affected cardiac tissue shows a granulomatous reaction with the presence of Aschoff bodies. Complications of rheumatic fever include mitral valve inflammation leading to long-term sequelae of chronic mitral valve regurgitation, prolapse, or stenosis. Treatment of the initial streptococcal infection is effective for reducing the risk for developing rheumatic fever. Per American Heart Association guidelines, once rheumatic fever has developed, treatment includes salicylates and a prolonged course of monthly penicillin treatments to reduce the risk for recurrence and further valvular damage.

During this time, he also has had dry, scaly, red patches of skin on his forearms and chest. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. During the past 2 years, he has worked as a restaurant dishwasher. A photograph of the left hand and right forearm is shown; similar findings are seen over the left forearm and trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.explanation: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition, often localized to sites of trauma, including the elbows and knees. Psoriasis is associated with production of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, interleukin (IL)-12, IL-17, and IL-23 produced by keratinocytes, dendritic cells, and T-cells. The Th17 lymphocyte is thought to be central to the pathophysiology of psoriasis, and newer biologic therapies target the cytokines released by these cells. Clinically, plaque psoriasis presents with thick, salmon-colored plaques on the extensor extremities with overlying silvery, white scale. Psoriasis may involve the nails, is associated with underlying psoriatic arthritis in a subset of patients, and, more recently, has been associated with the development of atherosclerotic disease. Treatments for psoriasis include topical steroids, topical calcipotriene (vitamin D analogue), narrowband UVB light therapy, and newer systemic biologic agents, including adalimumab, ixekizumab, secukinumab, and ustekinumab that specifically target different inflammatory pathways involved in psoriasis. This patient’s history of nail involvement and rash is clinically consistent with a diagnosis of psoriasis.

wrongAnswers.A: Atopic dermatitis (Choice A) and nummular eczema (Choice C), an atopic dermatitis variant, represent inflammatory skin conditions characterized by development of itching followed by rash. Atopic dermatitis may be associated with allergic rhinitis, asthma, and eosinophilic esophagitis. Atopic dermatitis is associated with itching and subsequent development of rough, lichenified plaques commonly found on flexural surfaces. Atopic dermatitis is treated with topical corticosteroids, topical calcineurin inhibitors, and dupilumab, an IL-4 and IL-13 inhibitor, in severe cases. Nummular eczema presents with pruritic, coin-shaped lesions on the extremities. It may be associated with venous stasis and xerosis and responds to similar treatments as atopic dermatitis. This patient’s condition is more consistent with psoriasis, given the clinical morphology of the lesions and nail involvement.
wrongAnswers.B: Hydradenitis suppurativa (Choice B) is an inflammatory condition of the skin, most commonly affecting apocrine gland-bearing areas, including the axillary, inguinal, anogenital, and inframammary areas. Pathogenesis is thought to involve occlusion of the follicular infundibulum followed by rupture of the hair follicle and development of inflammation. Clinically, hydradenitis presents with sterile abscesses in the intertriginous areas that may progress to scarring and sinus tract formation. Hydradenitis suppurativa treatments include weight reduction, smoking cessation, oral and topical antibiotic therapies, TNF-α inhibitors including adalimumab, and surgical excision. The absence of abscesses in this case makes hydradenitis suppurativa a less likely diagnosis.

The tonsils are mildly enlarged and erythematous; there is no exudate. There is postnasal drainage in the posterior pharynx and copious yellow-green nasal drainage. questions.subject: Otolaryngology
questions.explanation: Upper respiratory tract infections are common in children and infants. On average, children experience up to nine respiratory tract infections annually, and children who attend day care may experience more. This patient’s symptoms of nasal congestion, cough, sneezing, and nonexudative pharyngitis are consistent with a diagnosis of viral upper respiratory tract infection. The likelihood of group A streptococcal pharyngitis can be predicted with the Centor criteria (based on age, tonsillar exudates or swelling, lymphadenopathy, fever, and absence of cough). Most upper respiratory tract infections are caused by a virus and resolve with supportive care. However, specific upper respiratory tract infections, such as acute otitis media, bacterial sinusitis, and group A streptococcal pharyngitis benefit from treatment with antibiotics. This patient has normal mobile tympanic membranes, no fever, and nonexudative pharyngitis making acute otitis media, sinusitis, and streptococcal pharyngitis unlikely, so no antibiotics would be needed at this stage.
